sign.name: Sign Last
sign.tip: Your signature says the chart is complete. Sign after the handoff — every time.

vitals.name: Abnormal Vitals
vitals.tip: Abnormal is never 'stable.' Recheck it, write it, report it.

fullset.name: Full Set Every Time
fullset.tip: HR, BP, RR, SpO2 on every set, at least two sets, more on long rides.

impression.name: Impression Matcher
impression.tip: The impression is why they're on your cot — not 'No Apparent Illness.'

meds.name: Dose Detective
meds.tip: Drug, dose, units, route, time. Every med given before you arrived.

psych.name: Psych Pro
psych.tip: Legal status, safety search, SI details, guardian consent.

hospice.name: Code Status Keeper
hospice.tip: Every hospice/end-of-life transport: code status and DNR form travel with the patient.

narrative.name: No Templates
narrative.tip: Write what you found, not 'W/O INCIDENT' x7.

questions.prompt: Signing your crew attestation at dispatch is fine as long as you finish the chart later.
questions.explain: Your signature attests the chart is complete and accurate. In our October review, half of charts were signed before the crew even reached the scene.

questions.prompt: When should you sign the crew attestation on a BLS IFT?

options.text: When you open the chart at dispatch
After transfer of care, once you've reviewed the chart

questions.explain: Sign last. The attestation covers everything in the chart, including the handoff.

questions.prompt: Your partner wrote the chart, so your co-signature doesn't make you responsible for what's in it.
questions.explain: Your signature attests to the whole chart. Read it before you co-sign.

questions.prompt: Out of 35 charts reviewed in October, how many were signed BEFORE transfer of care?
questions.explain: 29 of 35 — and 18 of those before arriving on scene. This is our #1 system-wide fix.

questions.prompt: 16 y/o psych transfer. Tap the problem.

narrative.text: PATIENT WALKED FROM BED TO COT WITH EMS CREW.
PATIENT SECURED TO COT VIA SEATBELTS AND WINGS UP.
PATIENT CARE REPORT GIVEN TO NURSE.

questions.explain: 170/150 in a 16-year-old was never rechecked or mentioned. Recheck (manual if needed), document it, and report it to the receiving RN.

questions.prompt: Patient's HR was 116–120 the whole ride, but they 'looked fine,' so 'vitals remained stable' is accurate.
questions.explain: Persistent tachycardia is abnormal. Name it in the narrative, note what you did, and who you told.

questions.prompt: Pick the best rewrite: "PT VITALS AND CONDITION REMAINED STABLE THROUGHOUT TRANSPORT." (BP was 118/40, pt on warfarin)

options.text: Initial BP 118/40; recheck 120/45. Pt asymptomatic, A&Ox4, skin warm/dry. Low diastolic reported to receiving RN.
BP slightly low but pt is fine.

questions.explain: Name the abnormal value, show you rechecked it, describe how the patient looked, and say who you told.

questions.prompt: Chest pain, elevated troponin, BLS transfer. Tap the finding that was never mentioned in the narrative.

vitals.text: 1954 · HR 67 · BP 147/81 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · Pulse: IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR

narrative.text: DOCTOR CONFIRMED TRANSPORT IS BLS.
PT ABLE TO STAND AND SIT ON COT WITHOUT INCIDENT.
PT TRANSPORTED WITHOUT INCIDENT.

questions.explain: A new irregularly irregular pulse in a chest pain patient matters. Document it, ask if it's known, and report it.

questions.prompt: You get a reading you think is wrong (BP 170/150). Best move?

options.text: Delete it — it's obviously an artifact
Recheck (manual if possible), document both readings and your reasoning
Change it to the previous reading

questions.explain: Never delete or ignore a reading. Recheck it and write what you found — the chart has to explain itself.

questions.prompt: Post-op abdominal pain, IV Dilaudid given. Tap the problem.

narrative.text: PT HAS RECEIVED DILAUDID (1MG @ 1917), REGLAN, AND BENADRYL IN ER.
PT ABLE TO STAND WITH ASSISTANCE AND WALK TO COT.
MET WITH NURSE FOR REPORT AND PAPERWORK.

questions.explain: No blood pressure on either set — on a patient who just got IV opioids. Full set every time.

questions.prompt: A 2-hour, 115-mile psych transfer had vitals at 1223 and 1404. What's the problem?

options.text: Nothing — two sets is the minimum
A 100-minute gap with no reassessment on a long transport
Too many vitals for a psych patient
Vitals aren't needed on psych transfers

questions.explain: Two sets is the floor, not the goal. On long transports, reassess regularly per AMR KC guidelines.

questions.prompt: If the patient refuses a BP, leave the field blank.
questions.explain: Chart it as 'Refused' and note it in the narrative, plus what you could observe. A blank looks like you skipped it.

questions.prompt: What's a full set of vitals on a BLS transport?
questions.explain: HR, BP, RR, and SpO2 on every set — plus pain score when pain is part of the complaint.

questions.prompt: Hospice transport. SpO2 69% on room air, placed on NRB 15 LPM. Pick the best Primary Impression.
questions.explain: This chart was coded 'Weakness.' The impression should reflect why they needed you — here, the hypoxia.

questions.prompt: Colostomy dislodged at the nursing home; going to the ED for replacement. Best Primary Impression?
questions.explain: If they need an ambulance to the ED, 'No Apparent Illness' contradicts the call. Code the actual problem.

questions.prompt: Patient with 3rd-degree heart block, HR 75 the entire transport. Primary impression 'Bradycardia' is the best fit.
questions.explain: The documented HR doesn't support bradycardia. Use the rhythm (AV block, 3rd degree) — and make sure the numbers and the impression agree.

questions.prompt: Teen psych transfer for SI with a plan. Best Primary Impression?
questions.explain: 'No Apparent Illness' on an SI transfer undercuts medical necessity. Code the SI.

questions.prompt: Pick the best rewrite: "NURSE GAVE PATIENT .5 OF DILAUDID."

options.text: RN administered hydromorphone (Dilaudid) 0.5 mg IV at 1415 prior to EMS arrival.

questions.explain: Drug, dose, units, route, time. '.5' could be mg or mL — and a missing leading zero is a classic med-error setup.

questions.prompt: Tap the line with the documentation problem.

narrative.text: ER FOUND MODERATE SPINAL STENOSIS AT L3-L4 AND L4-L5.
PT WAS GIVEN MORPHINE (2 DOSES, LAST WAS 4 @ 2050) AND ZOFRAN.
ASSISTED PT IN STANDING AND PIVOTING WITH 2 PERSON ASSIST.

questions.explain: '4' of what? And Zofran has no dose or time. Units and route on every med.

questions.prompt: Meds given by the sending facility before you arrived don't need to be in your chart.
questions.explain: They affect your assessment (sedation, pain, vitals). Document drug, dose, units, route, and time.

questions.prompt: "Ativan and Haldol were given for agitation." What's missing?

options.text: Dose, route, and time for each

questions.explain: Sedatives given before transport change what you should expect en route. Dose, route, time.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the 4 must-haves on a psych transfer?
questions.explain: The 4: legal status, safety search, SI details, and who consented (for minors). Payer info goes in billing, not the narrative.

questions.prompt: SI with a plan to use a knife, auditory/visual hallucinations. What's MOST important that's missing?

narrative.text: PT WAS SEEN IN ED FOR SUICIDAL IDEATIONS W/ A PLAN TO USE A KNIFE.
PT IS MOVED FROM BED TO COT VIA WALKING W/O INCIDENT.
PT IS TRANSPORTED W/O INCIDENT.

questions.explain: With a weapon plan, the chart must show a safety search was done (and legal status). Tap the line that should have triggered it. Also: 160/95 never addressed.

questions.prompt: "Calm and cooperative, no interventions needed" is enough to show a psych patient needed an ambulance.
questions.explain: On its own, it argues they didn't. Add the reason: e.g., 'active SI with plan, requires 1:1 observation, elopement risk.'

questions.prompt: Best way to document this? The patient asks why he has to go, and the crew tells him they'd restrain him if he got aggressive.

options.text: Crew told pt we would restrain him.
Pt verbally agitated, questioning transport. Crew used calm verbal de-escalation and explained the process; pt agreed to sit on cot. No restraints required.
Leave it out of the chart.

questions.explain: Document the behavior, your de-escalation, and the outcome. Restraints are a protocol decision, not a threat to chart.

questions.prompt: 12 y/o SI transfer. Mom is at bedside. What should the chart say about consent?

options.text: Who consented (name and relationship) and that they signed as representative
Only needed if mom rides along

questions.explain: One of our best October charts did exactly this: named the parent and noted she signed as the patient's representative.

questions.prompt: In October's review, all 3 hospice transports documented the patient's code status.
questions.explain: None of them did. Every hospice/end-of-life transport: code status, and confirm the DNR/OOH-DNR form traveled with the patient.

questions.prompt: Hospice patient going home. Family member refuses vitals. What do you chart?

options.text: Who refused, their relationship, and what you could observe (resp effort, skin, mental status)

questions.explain: Refusals are documented, not blanks. Then chart what you can see without equipment.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in EVERY hospice transport chart?

options.text: Code status and that the DNR/OOH-DNR form traveled with the patient
Nothing extra — same as any transfer

questions.explain: If the patient deteriorates en route, the code status in your chart is what protects them and you.

questions.prompt: "ON SCENE, PRIMARY, HPI/PMH, SECONDARY, VITALS, PT TO COT" is an acceptable narrative.
questions.explain: That's a checklist, not a narrative. It says you did an assessment — but not what you found.

questions.prompt: Ventilator patient to an LTAC. Tap the biggest gap.

narrative.text: ARRIVED TO FIND MALE PT LYING SEMI FOWLERS IN BED.
PT UNABLE TO SPEAK AT THIS TIME DUE TO BEING ON A VENTILATOR.
PT RESPONSIVE TO VERBAL ONLY BUT DOES NOT SPEAK AT THIS TIME.
[ END OF NARRATIVE ]

questions.explain: The narrative ends before transport. No vent settings (mode, rate, TV, FiO2, PEEP), no reassessment, no handoff.

questions.prompt: Your narrative uses 'W/O INCIDENT' 7 times. What's the fix?

options.text: Say it once; use the space for findings — behavior, complaints, reassessment
Delete the narrative and rely on the fields
It's fine — it shows nothing went wrong

questions.explain: Swapping the phrase isn't a fix. Auditors and receiving staff need what you observed.

questions.prompt: "CREW STATED THEY DID NOT FEEL PAIN... CREW HAD A SLIGHT COUGH." — this clearly describes the patient.
questions.explain: As written, it says the crew had the pain and cough. Reread before you submit — pronouns matter in a legal record.

questions.prompt: Patient woke up with abnormal sensation in both legs and was incontinent without realizing it. Tap what's missing.

narrative.text: PT WAS INCONTINENT AS WELL WITHOUT REALIZING IT.
MET WITH PT WHO WAS ALERT AND PLEASANT.
[ NO NEURO EXAM DOCUMENTED ]
TRANSFERRED CARE, CLEANED EQUIPMENT, CLEARED SCENE.

questions.explain: New incontinence plus bilateral leg symptoms is a red flag. Document strength, sensation, and bowel/bladder function in both legs.
